## ABSTRACT

Commensal foraging is a positive interaction which occurs when one species benefits another's foraging activity without affecting their own. Though commensal relationships are widely recognized as ecologically important, instances of predator–predator commensalism remain relatively under documented in marine systems. Here, we report a predator–predator commensal foraging relationship between cobia (Rachycentron canadum), a pelagic marine ray-finned fish, and southern stingray (Hypanus americanus), a benthic whiptail stingray. While similar relationships have been documented between other teleost species and rays, there are few documented observations between cobia and southern stingrays. We observed this interaction during aerial drone surveys in a shallow, sandy-bottom habitat in Biscayne Bay, Florida, an atypical foraging environment for the offshore-associated cobia. Over the continuous 7-min and 13-s aerial observation, the cobia followed the stingray for > 90% of the time, closely tracking its position and shifting behavior based on the ray's activity. 2009; Knochel et al. 2023), freshwater (Ubaid 2011), and terrestrial (Hino 1998) ecosystems. These associations can shape community dynamics by enhancing feeding efficiency (Dickman 1992), altering predator–prey interactions, and facilitating resource access for opportunistic species (Bonham and Silbiger 2024; Kajiura et al. 2009). In particular, predator–predator commensalism, where one predatory species exploits the hunting behavior of another, represents a compelling example of behavioral plasticity and ecological interdependence. Because these interactions are often ephemeral, opportunistic, and difficult to detect, direct behavioral observations, especially in wild settings, can advance our understanding of the frequency, mechanisms, and ecological significance of commensal foraging. Here, we report a predator–predator commensal foraging association between cobia (Rachycentron canadum) and the southern stingray (Hypanus americanus).

Whiptail stingrays (family Dasyatidae), which comprise approximately 70 species distributed globally in tropical and subtropical waters, are particularly well known for their foraging strategy of undulating their pectoral fins and using their snouts to excavate the seafloor (Flowers et al. 2021; Freitas et al. 2019). This distinctive behavior generates feeding pits and sediment plumes that resuspend fine materials, mobilize organic matter, and facilitate nutrient exchange between the benthos and overlying water column (Giaroli et al. 2024; Grew et al. 2025). Quintessential examples of ecosystem engineers, stingrays can alter physical habitat structure (e.g., sediment composition and biogeochemical cycling) (Grew et al. 2025; Nauta et al. 2024) and ecosystem dynamics (e.g., distribution of infaunal and epifaunal organisms) (Flowers et al. 2021). In addition to their role as ecosystem engineers, stingrays and elasmobranchs more broadly have been documented as foraging facilitators for a range of ‘opportunistic foragers’. 2023). These relationships are not limited to elasmobranchs and teleosts; in Florida, double-crested cormorants (Nannopterum auritum) have been documented closely following a foraging southern stingray (H. americanus) and feeding on the small fish displaced by the ray's foraging (Kajiura et al. 2009).

The foraging activity of stingrays, through benthic disturbance and bioturbation, has been shown to facilitate access to buried prey and alter local ecological community structure (Giaroli et al. 2024), which may be exploited by opportunistic species like cobia (Rachycentron canadum). Cobia are marine predators widely distributed in subtropical and tropical waters, where they occupy mid- to upper trophic levels, feeding on marine vertebrates and invertebrates (Peterson et al. 2020). While much of the current research on cobia centers on their potential for aquaculture—owing to rapid growth rates, high fecundity, disease resistance, and strong feed-conversion efficiency—their natural behavior remains poorly understood (dos Santos Jύnior and de Nóbrega 2024). Indeed, relatively few studies address cobia's wild foraging strategies, habitat use, or interspecific interactions. Both at-sea and captive observations show that cobia frequently associate with large marine megafauna—including manta rays, sharks, large teleosts, and sea turtles—apparently to gain foraging or protective benefits (Braun et al. 2024; Crear et al. 2020; Félix and Hackradt 2008; Takamatsu 1967). This behavior has long been recognized as a form of commensalism (Shaffer and Nakamura 1989) and suggests that cobia may exploit the activities of larger animals to access prey or reduce predation risk. Although gut content analysis on cobia in Brazil suggested that they are primarily piscivorous predators across life stages (Hamilton et al. 2019), behavioral observations of foraging in the wild remain scarce. One of the few detailed examples comes from Smith and Merriner (1982), who reported cobia trailing cownose rays (Rhinoptera bonasus) and feeding on prey items that were disturbed—but not consumed—by the rays.

Given the opportunistic and transient nature of predator–predator commensalism, particularly involving large, mobile marine species, direct behavioral observations (i.e., natural history observations) are essential for identifying and characterizing these interactions (Anderson 2017). Despite growing anecdotal recognition of cobia's tendency to follow foraging megafauna, there remains a clear need for further documentation and description of such associations. For this reason, we detail and quantify the behaviors associated with a predator–predator commensal foraging interaction observed between cobia and a southern stingray in Biscayne Bay, FL.
